definition: Solipsistic means treating one's own mind or self as the only thing that truly exists or matters.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word solipsistic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know solipsistic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The band's documentary is oddly solipsistic — three of the four members appear only as elbows at the edge of the drummer's close-ups.
Self-absorbed people sink into their own concerns but can be pulled back out — the mildest rung, well below solipsistic.
Egocentric goes further than self-absorbed — every event measured by its effect on me — yet it still stops short of solipsistic, which quietly doubts the rest of you are fully there at all.

Self-centered people put their own needs and comfort first — the best seat, the last word, the bigger share. Solipsistic goes past grabbing into attention itself: the solipsistic speaker takes nothing from anyone; other people simply never come into focus as quite real.

Narcissistic means in love with your own image and hungry for admirers — the mirror, the applause, the follower count. Solipsistic needs no admirers, because it has forgotten the audience exists. A narcissist performs for the crowd; the solipsist no longer notices there is one.

Solipsistic means treating one's own mind or self as the only thing that truly exists or matters.
The captain's log from the disastrous voyage is notoriously solipsistic: the reef, the storm, and the mutinous crew each appear only as obstacles standing between the captain and his breakfast.
Solipsistic is more precise than 'selfish' because selfishness is about hoarding advantages; solipsism is about attention — behaving as if no mind but yours is quite real.
The solipsistic writer isn't cruel to other people; other people simply never come into focus.
Solipsistic is the heavyweight complaint about self-focus — reviews and essays use it when a work treats the world as scenery for one mind.
For garden-variety self-focus, 'self-centered' is honest and shorter.
Its unit-mate sophomoric mocks a different flaw: the sophomoric performer shows off badly for an audience; the solipsistic one has forgotten the audience exists.

The house that architect Renzo Vail built for himself in 1971 is often called the purest example of solipsistic design in the state.
Every measurement began and ended with Vail.
Counters sat at the height of his elbows, and the single reading chair faced away from the door.
Visitors noticed what was missing.
There was no guest room, no second chair, not even a coat hook that a caller might use.
Asked about it, Vail seemed genuinely puzzled.
Other people, one interviewer wrote, 'appeared never to have entered his calculations at all.' Admirers of the house praise its honesty.
Its critics answer that a home built as if no one else existed teaches a lesson no one should want.
